analysis.one_liner: Makes failed-bank executives and controlling shareholders repay up to three years of pay when their bank collapses.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to claw back pay from executives of failed big banks was referred to the Banking Committee on March 11, 2026 and has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: When an insured bank with more than $10 billion in assets fails and the FDIC takes it over, this bill would require the FDIC to claw back up to three years of compensation — salary, bonuses, stock awards, performance pay, and even profits from stock trading — from the bank's directors, officers, and controlling shareholders. The recovered money would go into the Deposit Insurance Fund, the government fund that backs customer deposits. It would also clarify the FDIC's power to recover compensation when it takes over a big financial company, no matter which legal process it used.
analysis.who_benefits: Depositors and taxpayers. The Deposit Insurance Fund pays out when banks fail, and money recovered from failed-bank executives would replenish it rather than leaving losses with the fund that backs everyone's insured deposits. It also raises the cost of failed leadership for executives at large banks, creating a reason to manage risk more carefully.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Depositors and the federal insurance fund

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDIC to claw back all or part of three years of compensation — salary, bonuses, equity awards, performance-based pay, and securities trading profits — from directors, officers, and controlling shareholders when an insured bank with more than $10 billion in assets fails and the FDIC becomes its receiver.
Any money clawed back must be deposited into the Deposit Insurance Fund, which stands behind insured customer deposits.

Amends the Dodd-Frank orderly liquidation authority so the FDIC can recover compensation from a failed financial company regardless of the process by which it was appointed receiver, closing a gap in recovery authority.

analysis.who_pays: Executives, directors, and controlling shareholders of large failed banks, who would repay up to three years of compensation. The banking industry broadly would face stricter consequences for failed leadership at big institutions.

drawbacks.text: The clawback applies only to banks with more than $10 billion in assets; executives of smaller failed banks would face no mandatory repayment.

The clawback is mandatory and covers all compensation types over a three-year lookback, including equity awards and stock-trading profits, which could sweep in pay from people the banking agency only determines after the fact were primarily responsible — inviting legal challenges and complicating compensation planning for large banks.
Clawing back pay after a failure recovers money but does not prevent bank failures or guarantee depositors are made whole; it is a remedy after losses occur, not a safeguard before them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — executives who run a large bank into the ground give back recent pay — is a straightforward accountability measure that the public generally favors, and it is funded at no cost to taxpayers. Its main limits are its narrow scope (big banks only) and the fact that it works after a failure rather than before. The chief cost is uncertainty and litigation risk for compensation at large banks.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote; Congress is still in session, so it could still move, but nothing is scheduled.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the Failed Bank Executives Clawback Act on March 11, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
Thirteen senators cosponsored the bill, including three Republicans — Josh Hawley, Katie Britt, and Kevin Cramer — giving it bipartisan support from the start.
No further action has been taken: the Banking Committee has not held a markup or scheduled the bill for a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one — the bill has not moved, and if it dies in committee, future failed-bank executives keep their pay and the Deposit Insurance Fund continues to absorb losses from big bank failures without recovery from those responsible.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one; the bill hasn't moved

sides.party_line_note: The bill is genuinely bipartisan: 13 cosponsors split 10 Democrats and 3 Republicans, though all action to date is the sponsor's introduction and referral.

industries.industry: Executives, directors, and controlling shareholders of large banks
industries.note: They would repay up to three years of compensation when a bank with more than $10 billion in assets fails and the FDIC takes it over. Their interest in blocking the bill runs directly against depositors and the insurance fund that backs them.

The bill imposes no new costs on healthy banks; it only triggers at failure, when executives and major shareholders of that institution owe money to the Deposit Insurance Fund. The main industry-wide effect is stricter accountability at the top of large institutions.

industries.industry: FDIC and the Deposit Insurance Fund
industries.note: The FDIC would gain a mandatory clawback tool and a new stream of recoveries deposited into the fund that backs insured deposits.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to Senate Banking with no committee action rarely reach the floor in the same Congress, even with bipartisan cosponsorship. The realistic path forward would be a burst of momentum after a high-profile bank failure, or inclusion of clawback language in a broader financial regulation package; on its own, the bill is likely to sit until the Congress ends unless the committee schedules a markup.
